summary: Plain C# countdown you tick yourself; exposes TimeRemaining, a 0-1 Progress, and start/complete events.
problem: Unity gives you coroutines and Invoke for "do this in N seconds", but neither hands you the remaining time, neither is easy to pause and resume, and each one spawns machinery you then have to cancel. CountdownTimer is a ~60-line object with no Unity dependency at all: you construct it, call Tick(deltaTime) from your own Update, and read TimeRemaining or Progress whenever you want to draw a bar. Because you supply the delta, you decide whether the timer obeys Time.timeScale (pass Time.deltaTime) or ignores a pause (pass Time.unscaledDeltaTime).

workedExample.setup: A 3-second ability cooldown driven from Update at a fixed 0.5 s step, then one longer step that overshoots zero.
steps: new CountdownTimer(3f) sets Duration = 3 but leaves TimeRemaining at 0 and IsRunning false, so Progress reads 1 - (0 / 3) = 1 before the timer has ever run.
timer.Start() assigns TimeRemaining = Duration = 3, sets IsRunning = true and fires OnStarted. Progress = 1 - (3 / 3) = 0.
Five calls to timer.Tick(0.5f) subtract 2.5 total: TimeRemaining = 3 - 2.5 = 0.5, and Progress = 1 - (0.5 / 3) = 0.8333.
timer.Tick(0.75f) computes TimeRemaining = 0.5 - 0.75 = -0.25. Because that is <= 0 it is clamped back to exactly 0, IsRunning flips to false, and OnCompleted fires once from inside Tick.
Progress is now 1 - (0 / 3) = 1. The 0.25 s of overshoot is discarded, not carried into the next Start().
workedExample.result: After 3.25 s of supplied delta the timer reports TimeRemaining 0, IsRunning false and Progress 1, having fired OnCompleted exactly once. Restarting from that handler loses up to one frame of time per cycle.

useCases: An ability or weapon cooldown whose remaining time drives a radial fill Image (Progress maps straight onto Image.fillAmount).
A round or match clock that must pause cleanly when the player opens a menu — Stop() freezes it, Resume() picks up mid-second.
A respawn or revive delay, where you also want to display "2.4s" rather than just be told when it is over.
Reusable per-enemy attack windup timers: one instance per agent, restarted with Start(newDuration) as the attack varies.
Anywhere you would otherwise write StartCoroutine + a bool flag + a cancellation check.

usage.codeNote: Start() and Start(float newDuration) are real public methods on the class even though the member table below omits them (an extractor gap, not a missing API). The float overload reassigns Duration, so one instance can serve a different cooldown length each time.

apiNotes.Duration: The full length the timer was constructed with, or last restarted with via Start(newDuration). Only ever written by the constructor and that overload — Tick never touches it, which is what makes Progress a stable 0-1 ratio.
apiNotes.TimeRemaining: Counts down in whatever units you feed Tick. Clamped to exactly 0 on completion, so it never goes negative and you can compare it to 0 safely.
apiNotes.IsRunning: False before the first Start(), false after Stop(), and false the instant TimeRemaining hits 0. Tick() returns immediately when it is false, so a finished or paused timer costs nothing.
apiNotes.Progress: 1 - (TimeRemaining / Duration), guarded so a Duration of 0 or less reports 1 instead of dividing by zero. 0 at the moment of Start, 1 at completion — note it also reads 1 on a freshly constructed timer that has never started.
apiNotes.OnStarted: Fires at the end of Start(), after TimeRemaining and IsRunning have already been set, so a handler can read the fresh state. There is no unsubscribe helper; you hold the -= yourself.
apiNotes.OnCompleted: Fires from inside Tick(), after TimeRemaining is clamped to 0 and IsRunning is set false. Calling Start() from this handler is the supported way to loop (the demo runner does exactly that).
apiNotes.Stop(): A pause, not a reset: it only clears IsRunning and deliberately leaves TimeRemaining where it was. Pair with Resume() to continue, or Start() to go back to the full Duration.
apiNotes.Resume(): Sets IsRunning true only if TimeRemaining > 0. After a completed timer this is a no-op — an intentional guard so a stray Resume() cannot un-finish a timer that already fired OnCompleted.
apiNotes.Tick(float): The entire engine of the class. Does nothing unless IsRunning, subtracts the delta, and on crossing zero clamps, stops and raises OnCompleted in that order. Call it exactly once per frame per timer; calling it twice halves the effective duration.

gotchas.title: Progress is 1 before the first Start()
gotchas.body: A freshly constructed timer has TimeRemaining = 0, and Progress is defined as 1 - TimeRemaining/Duration, so it reports 1 ("finished"). A fill bar bound to Progress in Awake shows completely full until something calls Start(). Either call Start() during setup or gate the UI on IsRunning.

gotchas.title: Resume() cannot restart a finished timer
gotchas.body: Resume() only re-arms when TimeRemaining > 0, and a completed timer sits at exactly 0. Calling Resume() there does nothing and fails silently. Use Start() (or Start(newDuration)) to run it again.

gotchas.title: Overshoot is thrown away, so loops drift
gotchas.body: When a Tick pushes TimeRemaining past zero, the excess is clamped off rather than carried over. A timer that restarts itself from OnCompleted therefore loses up to one frame per cycle — at 60 fps and a 1 s loop that is roughly 1.6% slow, and it accumulates. For anything that must stay in step with wall-clock time, track a target timestamp instead.

gotchas.title: Nothing ticks it for you
gotchas.body: This is not a MonoBehaviour and starts no coroutine. If the component that owns it is disabled, its Update stops and the timer simply freezes mid-count — usually what you want, but it means the timer is not a wall clock. It is also only as pause-aware as the delta you pass: Time.deltaTime honours Time.timeScale = 0, Time.unscaledDeltaTime ignores it.

gotchas.title: Event handlers stack on a reused instance
gotchas.body: There is no Reset or Clear. If you keep one timer for the lifetime of a component and subscribe to OnCompleted each time you Start() it, every restart adds another handler and the callback fires N times. Subscribe once, in Awake or Start.
